https://www.dw.com/en/how-does-eastern-e.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5I36F August 2 marks the European Roma Holocaust Memorial Day, when Europe honors the memory of the victims and survivors of the Roma and Sinti genocide under Nazi Germany Image: Jacek Bednarczyk/dpa/picture alliance Advertisement It took decades before Germany recognized the Romani Holocaust — the Nazi genocide of 500,000 European Roma and Sinti during World War II . Several more decades passed before the European Holocaust Memorial Day for Sinti and Roma became an official German and European day of remembrance, celebrated each year on August 2. Based on initiatives by Polish Roma groups, the Nazi liquidation of the so-called "Gypsy Family Camp" in the Auschwitz-Birkenau Concentration and Extermination Camp on the evening of August 2-3, 1944, was first commemorated half a century later, in 1994. Germany marks the European Roma Holocaust Memorial Day on August 2 Image: Joerg Carstensen/dpa/picture alliance Thousands of deported Roma and Sinti had already been killed as a result of malnutrition and disease. That evening, thousands more were forced into gas chambers, shot and beaten to death by Nazi henchmen. In 2015, the European Parliament declared this date the European Roma Holocaust Memorial Day. In Germany and other European countries, the genocide is commemorated by officials with the participation of government representatives. In some cases, representatives of European governments travel to the memorial site in Auschwitz. In most cases, however, countries hold their own memorial services — particularly in central and southeastern Europe, where Nazi extermination commonly targeted Romani peoples . These days, such memorial days also take the opportunity to raise awareness for ongoing Antiziganism and the consequences it has. Roma, Sinti persecuted in WWII still fight for recognition To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Poland: 15 years of commemoration Poland , home to an estimated 30,000 Roma, has been observing August 2 since 2011. The ceremony routinely includes a visit by parliamentary and governmental representatives to the Auschwitz Memorial. Another important day of remembrance is observed each year in the village of Szczurowa, east of Krakow, on July 3. It honors the memory of Polish Roma massacred by German troops in 1943. In 1956, Szczurowa became the first site of a European memorial for victims of the Romani Holocaust. Other small towns and villages across southeastern Poland also commemorate the killing of Polish Roma during Nazi German occupation. Czechia: A former pig farm turned memorial site In the Czech Republic , where nearly 250,000 Roma live, August 2 has been an official day of remembrance since 2015. The most important ceremony is held in Lety, south of Prague, where Roma organizations have been commemorating the genocide for decades. This is the site where German Nazis established a concentration camp in 1940, and began deporting and imprisoning Romani families from occupied Bohemia from 1942 onward. After the war, the site was used as a pig farm. It was closed in 2018, following a long controversy , and transformed into a place of remembrance. Czech President Petr Pavel and then-Prime Minister Petr Fiala both attended the opening ceremony in April 2024. Another memorial site is located in Hodonin north of Brno, at the location of a further Nazi concentration camp which imprisoned Romani people from Bohemia and Moravia. Here, one of the atrocities commemorated includes the mass deportation of Roma and Sinti to Auschwitz on August 21, 1943. The site of the former concentration camp in Lety had been used as a pig farm after World War II Image: Lubos Palata/DW Slovakia: Memorial Day established in 2005 Around half a million Roma live in Slovakia . Here, the Romani Holocaust Memorial Day has been observed on August 2 since 2005. The main ceremony is held at the Slovak National Uprising (SNU) museum in Banska Bystrica in central Slovakia. The museum honors the 1944 armed uprising against Nazi occupation. It was one of the largest anti-fascist movements in Europe during World War II. The memorial ceremony is organized by the government's Plenipotentiary for Romani Communities and non-governmental Roma initiatives. Other representatives of the state or the presidential office also take part. Hungary: Antiziganism yesterday and today Around 600,000 Roma call Hungary home. Here, since 2005, various sites have been observing the Romani Holocaust Memorial Day on August 2, following a parliamentary resolution. In Budapest alone, there are three places of remembering for the Roma murdered during the Holocaust where commemorative events are held. The reason for these and numerous other memorial sites is that Hungarian Roma were the target of deportations and killings particularly following German occupation in 1944 and under the rule of the Arrow Cross, Hungary's fascist regime. Historical remembrance in Hungary is also deeply intertwined with the racist murdering spree directed at Roma people between 2008 and 2009. In this time, four Hungarian neo-Nazis killed a total of six people and injured 55 others, some of them severely. They planned their final hate crime for the night of August 2, in the eastern village of Kisleta. After Orban, Hungary's Roma hope for change To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Romania: Deportation to Transnistria Romania , where around 2 million Roma live, Roma Holocaust Memorial Day has officially been observed since 2020. The main event is held at the Holocaust Memorial in Bucharest, which was inaugurated in 2009. Under the dictator Ion Antonescu, who was allied with Nazi Germany, Romania independently organized the mass deportation of Jews and Roma to Transnistria , where about 380,000 Jews and 11,000 Roma were murdered in camps or died from hunger and disease. In 2025, President Nicusor Dan became the first Romanian head of state to personally attend the memorial service. In 2004, Romania designated October 9 as its official Holocaust Remembrance Day. It was on that day that Jewish citizens were first deported from the Bukovina region to Transnistria. The day also explicitly honors the memory of Roma who were deported and murdered by Antonescu's regime. Bulgaria: Commemoration without day of remembrance About 700,000 Roma call Bulgaria home. Here, August 2 has yet to be declared an official day of remembrance, but it is still marked with commemorative events organized by Roma organizations. Government and state representatives also take the occasion to issue commemorative statements. Although Bulgaria was allied with Nazi Germany, it resisted German demands to deport Jews and Roma. But groups were discriminated against through a wide range of racist laws, and effectively made second-class citizens. Croatia: Focus on escape attempt Croatia has a population of about 25,000 Roma. Its parliament only declared August 2 a day of remembrance in 2014. The main commemorative ceremony is held at the site of the former concentration and extermination camp Jasenovac , where the fascist Ustashe movement imprisoned Serbs, Jews, Croats and Roma. Between 15,000 and 20,000 were murdered there. High-ranking politicians regularly take part in commemorative ceremonies. More broadly, remembrance events in Jasenovac primarily highlight April 22, when prisoners attempted to escape the extermination camp in 1945. Croatia’s shadows of the past To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video North Macedonia: Memorial Day and national holiday Around 100,000 Roma live in North Macedonia , where the Roma Holocaust Memorial Day has officially been observed on August 2 since 2017. A key remembrance ceremony is held in Skopje at the Holocaust Memorial Center for the Jews of Macedonia. In North Macedonia is also a national and religious holiday: Republic Day and St Elijah Day, respectively. because of this, public remembrance of the Roma genocide tends to receive less attention. Serbia: No official day of remembrance In Serbia , home to around 130,000 Roma, August 2 is not an official memorial day for the Roma genocide. But there are other days of remembering the genocidal policies of the Nazi and Ustase regimes which also honor the memory of the Roma killed in the genocide. This article was translated from German. Photograph: Ronnie Amini/AAP View image in fullscreen Three men charged over the alleged home invasions in Arncliffe and Bankstown were due to face court on Friday. Photograph: Ronnie Amini/AAP Sydney Women hospitalised and three men charged with assault and choking after separate home invasions in Sydney NSW police allege the men, aged 18, 19 and 20, broke into homes in Arncliffe and Bankstown this week before assaulting the women aged 31 and 32 Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Adeshola Ore Thu 1 Oct 2026 22.34 EDT First published on Thu 1 Oct 2026 21.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Three men have been detained after two women were allegedly assaulted during separate home invasions in Sydney’s south-west. New South Wales police were called to a home invasion in Arncliffe at about midnight on Tuesday morning. Officers were told a group of men forced entry into the home and threatened a 31-year-old woman with a knife before sexually assaulting her and stealing money. The woman, who didn’t know the men, was taken to hospital with “minor injuries”, police said on Friday. Officers separately responded to a reported home invasion at a unit in Bankstown at about 12.30am on Thursday, police said. Matt Kean warns climate crisis ‘isn’t someone else’s problem’ as largest coal project in NSW history greenlit Read more Police were told three men allegedly forced entry into the unit before assaulting a 32-year-old woman and stealing money. The woman, who again didn’t know the men, was taken to hospital for treatment of minor injuries, police said. Sex Crimes Squad Commander Det Supt Virginia Gorman said police believe the three men had planned the offences. “I believe that these men had done some research and they believed that these women might be home alone and they might have money on the premises. So they were specifically targeted,” she said. Speaking to reporters, Gorman described the alleged offences as “very violent”. “Excessively violent for three men armed with a weapon against vulnerable women home alone,” she said. “They were armed with a knife. They used duct tape to restrain them. They had duct tape over their mouths. They assaulted the women, punching a woman. You don’t need to do that to overcome a solo female. The violence is over the top for what they’ve done.” Detectives, supported by the riot squad, subsequently raided three properties in Belmore, Punchbowl and Greenacre at about 7.45pm on Thursday. A 20-year-old man arrested in Belmore was charged with aggravated break and enter, depriving a person of their liberty, choking and common assault, along with other offences. A 19-year-old man arrested in Punchbowl and charged with aggravated break and enter, choking and aggravated sexual assault, along with other offences. An 18-year-old man arrested in Greenacre was charged with aggravated break and enter, choking and common assault, along with other offences. Gorman said the men will be prosecuted to the full extent of the law. “The offences are very serious … because the violence they committed was of the highest order.” All three men were due to face local courts on Friday. https://www.politico.eu/article/eu-count.text: BRUSSELS — The EU will only conduct further releases of oil and diesel reserves after the International Energy Agency has made it clear such a move would not be damaging to the bloc's energy security, three diplomats familiar with the matter told POLITICO. The Group of Seven — which includes Italy, Japan, Germany the U.K., France and the U.S. — agreed on Friday to release 100 million barrels of oil and diesel after U.S. officials threatened to ban diesel exports if they didn't tap stockpiles. However, the IEA appeared to confirm Wednesday that that release would draw from stocks pledged under an agreement in March and not include additional supplies. In other words, it would not amount to a new release at all, but would simply fulfil prior promises. Advertisement Advertisement In a meeting Wednesday afternoon, EU officials endorsed the position, pledging to defer any future drawdowns "pending a clearer IEA assessment of market conditions and security-of-supply risks," said one of the diplomats. Countries need to know "how low we can go," said another. While diesel prices are high as a result of airstrikes on energy infrastructure in Russia and the Middle East, some EU countries warned that releasing stocks now could leave them vulnerable in the event of a supply crisis. There remain enough untapped stocks among IEA members to satisfy the pledge to release 100 million barrels. Of the 400 million barrels pledged in March, 325 million have been released, with some countries releasing "greater volumes than they initially pledged," the IEA said in a statement following an emergency ministerial meeting. That leaves around 100 million left that countries can still release under that agreement, it added. It said the fresh commitment would represent a "completion" of that March agreement. The IEA's 32 members include wealthy European, North American and East Asian countries. POLITICO reported earlier Wednesday that France and Germany — which hold some of Europe's most significant stockpiles — had signalled they would release no or minimal supplies on top of those already pledged. It remains unclear what share of the releases non-EU members of the IEA will accept, after Japan, another member, ruled out any further releases. Further details on the breakdown of the G7 release will be discussed at a meeting of the IEA's governing board next week, the second diplomat said. Advertisement Advertisement

Photograph: Mark Richardson/Alamy View image in fullscreen ‘If we do not tag them as they leave prison, there is a good chance that we won’t tag them at all,’ said one senior probation worker. Photograph: Mark Richardson/Alamy Prisons and probation Hundreds of early-release prisoners in England and Wales not being tagged, say MPs Serco denies tagging failures as police and probation officers struggle to cope with influx of released offenders Rajeev Syal and Jamie Grierson Tue 13 Oct 2026 12.03 EDT Last modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 13.40 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Hundreds of prisoners released early across England and Wales, including stalkers and violent offenders, are not being tagged, MPs have said, despite promises of the “toughest supervision in British history”. As the government begins releasing a second tranche of 650 offenders to relieve prison overcrowding, police and probation officers have said they are struggling to cope with a new influx of offenders who are supposed to be monitored in the community. Speaking during an urgent question in the Commons on Tuesday, the Labour MP Clive Efford asked why the outsourcing company Serco had failed to tag prisoners as they leave prison. Serco has denied any such failure. “They are not actually fulfilling their contracts. It can’t be beyond the tech firm’s ability to tag people on release. So what are these companies going to do about it?” he said. The shadow justice secretary, Nick Timothy, said most prisoners were not being tagged before release, despite assurances from the government that the tagging system would be the “toughest in history”. Prisoners thank Andy Burnham as they leave jail in first wave of early releases Read more “The justice secretary told the country that proper safeguards would be put in place with a presumption that all released prisoners would be tagged. He called it the toughest tagging regime in history, but that was nonsense,” he said. Jake Richards, the justice minister, replied: “We are working closely with Serco and have seen an improvement in the implementation since March this year. Although there is a presumption of every person being tagged, ultimately it is an operational decision.” A Serco spokesperson said it is “delivering an excellent service, tagging a record number of people, and consistently meeting all our contractual measures”. The spokesperson added: “The Ministry of Justice has publicly recognised the quality of our performance and our team has successfully delivered four early release schemes. “We attempt to fit an electronic monitoring device to every person required to wear one. Where it is not possible to fit a device, or where the person breaches the conditions of their release, the individual is reported to the relevant authorities, who are responsible for considering and taking any further action.” About 2,000 criminals, including domestic abusers and violent offenders, are being freed this month, with another 3,000 to follow in stages over the next year. The total was reduced from 6,000 after an intervention by Andy Burnham . Prisoners convicted of manslaughter are excluded, meaning the killers of PC Andrew Harper, who died in the line of duty in 2019, will not be eligible. Typically, those being released should expect to be electronically tagged and subject to other monitoring conditions for the second third of their sentence. But the probation service union, Napo, said the releases were putting enormous strain on its members, who monitor offenders in the community. The union held a pre-ballot meeting on Tuesday concerning taking strike action over pay and workloads. Pay negotiations ended earlier in October with a “best and final” conditional pay offer worth 5%, which the union’s negotiating committee rejected. Members will be asked to vote for industrial action on pay, along with a question on workloads, in a formal ballot on industrial action to launch on 19 October. The union says probation officers have been required to take on large amounts of extra work since tens of thousands of prisoners began being released early in 2022. A senior Prison and Probation Service source said a failure to place tags on released offenders as they left prison meant it could then be up to a month before they were tagged. “If we do not tag them as they leave prison, there is a good chance that we won’t tag them at all before they reoffend,” they said. Mark Rowley, the Metropolitan police commissioner, said many of those who breached their tagging conditions – by consuming alcohol or drugs, or by breaching a curfew, for example – were not facing sanctions if arrested. “We’re seeing 95%-plus of the tagging breaches that we arrest are simply being bailed back into the community on the same condition. So there is zero sanction,” he said. The number of people in prison has jumped by more than 1,700 in the past three months. The prison population in England and Wales was at 87,499 on Monday, according to Ministry of Justice data, up from 85,761 on 29 June, a rise of 2%. Alex Norris, the justice secretary, has said released offenders will be monitored under the “toughest supervision in British history” . New restriction zones designed to control the movements of the highest-risk sexual and violent offenders should confine released prisoners to areas a few miles wide, in an effort to reassure their victims. However, this month the victims’ commissioner, Claire Waxman, said the government’s confidence in the plan was “not yet matched by the reality on the ground”. You may follow him at Twitter @FidelRahmati Lithuanian border guards detained 35 migrants after they crossed into Lithuania from Belarus in the Varėna district, authorities said, as the country continues to monitor irregular migration along its eastern border. The group was detected Thursday evening near the village of Katra in the Čepkeliai Nature Reserve after a border surveillance system identified the crossing. The migrants split into several groups after entering Lithuania, but border guards detained all 35 before they could move deeper into the country. The State Border Guard Service (VSAT) said the operation involved a helicopter, service dogs, police officers and personnel from several border-guard units. The helicopter helped locate groups that had dispersed through the forest and marshland. All 35 detainees were men between about 20 and 30 years old. Eleven had identification documents, while the others had no documents. During questioning, they identified themselves as citizens of Afghanistan and Iraq, according to Lithuanian authorities. By Friday morning, 29 of the migrants had been denied entry and returned to Belarus under Lithuanian procedures. Questioning of five others was continuing, while another migrant who reported feeling unwell was taken to a medical facility for examination. Authorities said the group did not resist during the detention operation. The incident took place in a section of the Lithuania-Belarus border where fencing cannot be installed because of unstable ground and difficult natural conditions. Lithuanian border guards therefore rely on surveillance systems and other measures to monitor the area. Lithuanian authorities said they have prevented 1,661 migrant s from entering the country illegally from Belarus at unauthorized locations so far this year. The figure compares with 1,652 such attempts prevented in 2025 and 1,002 in 2024. The Lithuania-Belarus border has remained a major migration route toward the European Union since a wider migration crisis began in 2021. Lithuanian and other EU authorities have repeatedly strengthened border controls and surveillance in response to continued attempts to cross from Belarus. https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text: Student List supporters in Belgrade react to the rightwing Serbian Progressive party conceding defeat on Sunday. Photograph: Marko Drobnjaković/AP View image in fullscreen Student List supporters in Belgrade react to the rightwing Serbian Progressive party conceding defeat on Sunday. Photograph: Marko Drobnjaković/AP Opinion Serbia As students we never sought power – here’s how we reclaimed Serbia Novak Simin After freedom, we want to give our people something radical: a normal, functioning state Mon 26 Oct 2026 15.04 EDT Last modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 17.56 EDT Share T wo years ago, I harboured no political ambition whatsoever. I was a student at the faculty of technical sciences in Novi Sad, my home town, pursuing a PhD in human resources and simply living my life. That was until the canopy collapse at the newly renovated train station in Novi Sad in November 2024, which killed 16 people. I took part in street protests and rallies in response to this shocking event, and like many others, realised that it needed to be a turning point. This was not an unavoidable tragedy. Systemic corruption and a culture of entrenched impunity were obvious factors in the collapse. But instead of ordering a full and impartial investigation and coming clean on official failings, the authorities began pushing back against us for demanding justice. We were vilified and attacked in the streets but law enforcement did nothing. So we took refuge in our lecture halls and schools, barricading ourselves inside faculty buildings, ready for a long haul. Democratic principles have long been ignored in Serbia but we made sure we observed them in our gatherings. As our coordination developed, we made sure we had the same clear goal for every demonstration we organised: pressuring a corrupt government to meet our demands. And these were demands that in any free country would have been accepted automatically. We wanted, for example, all the documentation concerning the renovation of Novi Sad railway station to be made public, without redaction, and that everyone responsible for the works be held to account. We demanded that those who assaulted us in the streets be arrested and prosecuted. Instead of agreeing, state officials began branding us fascists and traitors . I was personally targeted for speaking out. As I handled media relations and communications, this often meant giving interviews to the country’s few remaining independent outlets. For this, I was accused by the regime’s propaganda machine of money laundering “millions” and conspiring with foreign powers. Others had to leave the country after being accused of high treason; some spent months in detention on manufactured, illegally obtained evidence. Many of us were placed under surveillance, our parents threatened, and many were fired from jobs and dragged through the mud in the pro-government popular press. But none of that intimidation broke us; rather it hardened our resolve. And eventually, when it became clear the regime would never concede, we opted to enter the electoral arena ourselves. That was the genesis of the Student List . Through open, democratic plenary sessions, we nominated individuals of integrity and competence, people who were committed to justice and freedom for a silenced society. Our aims were clear and never wavered: we wanted Serbia to be governed by the rule of law, independent public institutions, transparency and solidarity in a fractured nation. We marched thousands of kilometres across Serbia, campaigning relentlessly and in doing so helped, I believe, to rekindle hope among the broader public. State propaganda could not hope to drown out that much unfiltered grassroots momentum. Now the regime has fallen, our collective effort to rebuild Serbia begins. True, sceptics may argue that we have filled parliament with political novices. The truth is that we have filled it with people eager to serve and willing to learn. Our newly elected representatives are professors, doctors, lawyers, farmers and scientists, all experts in their fields. Each has an established record of honest work and civic integrity. They may lack traditional political backgrounds, but they have spent the past two years studying the realities of governance and public trust. That very lack of direct political involvement is why the Serbian people have placed their faith in us: they did not vote for slick rhetoric or cynical manoeuvreing. They voted for clean hands. We are neither promising, nor expecting overnight miracles as a result of this victory; rather we hope for something fundamentally radical for Serbia: normal, functioning institutions. This mandate must first of all dismantle the culture of impunity. That requires verifiably independent prosecutors, fully transparent public procurement processes, and legal accountability for anyone who treated state resources as private spoils. For too long our teachers, healthcare workers and civil servants have seen their expertise subordinated to party loyalty cards. We want to restore the dignity of these dedicated public servants. We have taken our country back, and are proud to stand as free citizens of Serbia. If this historic turning point proves anything, it is that this country does not belong to an untouchable ruling elite. It belongs to all of us. We have proven that dignity is non-negotiable. Now, the real work begins. This victory marks the end of institutional fear. For the first time in years, we can breathe freely. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion Novak Simin is a member of Serbia’s Student List movement Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? https://www.thehindu.com/news/national/p.text: WARSAW/NEW DELHI After Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s recent visit to India, the first by a Polish PM in 16 years, the India-Polish “strategic partnership” is expected to get stronger through better economic and defence cooperation. This comes two years after Prime Minister Narendra Modi visited Poland in 2024, which was the first visit by an Indian PM in 45 years, during which the relationship was elevated to “strategic partnership”.
